source: Care Quality Commission, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, Regulation 17: Good governance, regulation 17(2)(c) (CQC guidance page, updated May 2025, accessed 2026)
wording: maintain securely an accurate, complete and contemporaneous record in respect of each service user, including a record of the care and treatment provided to the service user and of decisions taken in relation to the care and treatment provided

source: Care Quality Commission, Regulation 20: Duty of candour, 'What you must do when you discover a notifiable safety incident' (accessed 2026)
wording: You must start the specific procedure laid out in the duty of candour regulation ‘as soon as reasonably practicable’.

source: Resuscitation Council UK, Quality standards: Acute care, section 5 The resuscitation team (2013, last updated July 2023, accessed 2026)
wording: The organisation must ensure that the resuscitation team is activated within 30 seconds of the call for help. This system must be tested daily.

source: Resuscitation Council UK, Quality standards: Acute care, section 5 The resuscitation team (2013, last updated July 2023, accessed 2026)
wording: The organisation must ensure that a complete and detailed record of the cardiorespiratory arrest is retained within the patient’s clinical record.

source: Royal College of Surgeons of England, Good Surgical Practice (2025), Domain 3, section 3.5 Record your work clearly, accurately and legibly (accessed 2026)
wording: Ensure that when members of the surgical team make case note entries these are legibly signed and show the date, and in cases in which the clinical condition is changing, the correct time.

source: Royal College of Surgeons of England, Good Surgical Practice (2025), Domain 3, section 3.5 Record your work clearly, accurately and legibly, operative notes (accessed 2026)
wording: Ensure that there are clear (preferably typed) operative notes for every procedure. The notes should accompany the patient into recovery and to the ward and should give sufficient detail to enable continuity of care by another doctor.

source: Royal College of Surgeons of England, Good Surgical Practice (2025), Domain 2, section 2.4 Shared decision making and consent (accessed 2026)
wording: Obtain the patient’s consent prior to surgery and ensure that the patient has sufficient time for reflection and sufficient information to make an informed decision. A patient’s consent should not be taken in the anaesthetic room.

source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for interpretation and reporting of imaging investigations, third edition (October 2025), section 05 The report, general considerations (accessed 2026)
wording: Clinical details should form part of the report. Interpretation may be incorrect if referral details are deficient, absent or misleading; inclusion of the referrer’s text is recommended as it may be a consideration for future review.

source: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for interpretation and reporting of imaging investigations, third edition (October 2025), section 01 Introduction (accessed 2026)
wording: Where the imaging interpretation is delegated to the referrer (eg orthopaedic surgeons, where a formal radiology report is not required), written documentation of the interpretation should be recorded in the patient’s notes by the referrer to satisfy the requirements of the Ionising Radiation (Medical Exposure) Regulations (IR(ME)R).

source: Department of Health (Ireland), NCEC National Clinical Guideline No. 1, Irish National Early Warning System (INEWS) V2, summary, recommendation 5 (September 2020, accessed 2026)
wording: In the acute setting the minimum standard for the assessment of observations is every six hours for the first 24 hours following admission and a minimum of every 12 hours monitoring thereafter if the patient’s clinical condition dictates.

source: Department of Health (Ireland), NCEC National Clinical Guideline No. 1, Irish National Early Warning System (INEWS) V2, summary, recommendation 17 (September 2020, accessed 2026)
wording: The modified INEWS Escalation and Response Protocol should be reviewed by a Registrar or Consultant doctor every 24 hours and documented on the INEWS observation chart.

source: RCEM Best Practice Guideline: Management of Acute Pain in Adults in the Emergency Department, summary of recommendations, recommendation 2 (September 2024, accessed 2026)
wording: All emergency departments should ensure patients with moderate and severe pain receive adequate analgesia within 15 minutes of arrival.

source: RCEM Best Practice Guideline: Management of Acute Pain in Adults in the Emergency Department, summary of recommendations, recommendation 12 (September 2024, accessed 2026)
wording: The duration of discharge opioid prescriptions for acute pain should ideally be limited to 3-5 days (although may be extended up to 7 days in specific circumstances such as predictable gaps in access to healthcare).

source: NHS Services, Seven Days a Week Forum, Seven Day Services Clinical Standards, Standard 2 Time to first consultant review (revised February 2016; National Archives copy, accessed 2026)
wording: All emergency admissions must be seen and have a thorough clinical assessment by a suitable consultant as soon as possible but at the latest within 14 hours from the time of arrival at hospital.

source: NHS Services, Seven Days a Week Forum, Seven Day Services Clinical Standards, Standard 4 Shift handovers (revised February 2016; National Archives copy, accessed 2026)
wording: Handovers must be led by a competent senior decision maker and take place at a designated time and place, with multi-professional participation from the relevant in-coming and out-going shifts. Handover processes, including communication and documentation, must be reflected in hospital policy and standardised across seven days of the week.

source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 47, Blood Transfusion in Obstetrics, consent for blood transfusion (May 2015, accessed 2026)
wording: The reason for transfusion and a note of the consent discussion should be documented in the patient’s case notes.

source: FSRH Clinical Guideline: Intrauterine Contraception (March 2023, amended January 2025), suggested auditable standard 4 (accessed 2026)
wording: Following insertion, 100% of individuals should be given information on the device inserted, including the name of the device, its duration of use and whether it can be relied upon immediately for contraception or if other precautions are required.

source: Royal Pharmaceutical Society and Royal College of Nursing, Professional Guidance on the Administration of Medicines in Healthcare Settings (January 2019), principle 17.2 (accessed 2026)
wording: Where a medicine is not administered or refused, details of the reason why (if known) are included in the record and, where appropriate, the prescriber multidisciplinary team is notified in accordance with the organisation policies and procedures.

source: Nursing and Midwifery Council, The Code: Professional standards of practice and behaviour for nurses, midwives and nursing associates, standard 10.4 (2015, updated 2018, accessed 2026)
wording: attribute any entries you make in any paper or electronic records to yourself, making sure they are clearly written, dated and timed, and do not include unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation

source: Royal College of Physicians, Generic medical record keeping standards (webpage dated October 2015, accessed 2026)
wording: Every entry in the medical record should be dated, timed (24 hour clock), legible and signed by the person making the entry. The name and designation of the person making the entry should be legibly printed against their signature.

source: Royal College of Physicians, Generic medical record keeping standards, frequency of entries (webpage dated October 2015, accessed 2026)
wording: An entry should be made in the medical record whenever a patient is seen by a doctor. When there is no entry in the hospital record for more than four days for acute medical care or seven days for long-stay continuing care, the next entry should explain why.

source: Royal College of Psychiatrists CCQI, Standards for Inpatient Mental Health Services, fourth edition (2022), standard 2.5 (accessed 2026)
wording: Patients have a comprehensive physical health review. This is started within four hours of admission, or as soon as is practically possible.

source: Royal College of Psychiatrists CCQI, Standards for Inpatient Mental Health Services, fourth edition (2022), standard 9.4 (accessed 2026)
wording: The team makes sure that patients who are discharged from hospital have arrangements in place to be followed up within 72 hours of discharge.

source: RCPCH Facing the Future: Standards for Acute General Paediatric Services, second of the ten standards listed on the RCPCH page (tier two review within four hours) (2015, accessed 2026)
wording: Every child who is admitted to a paediatric department with an acute medical problem is seen by a healthcare professional with the appropriate competencies to work on the tier two (middle grade) paediatric rota within four hours of admission.
